questions.question: What is the total number of airway divisions present in between trachea and alveolar sacs?
questions.explanation:
The total number of airway generations present in between the trachea and alveolar sac is 23.
The tracheobronchial tree is divided into multiple generations based on Weibel’s lung model. It
begins at the trachea (designated as zero) and ends with alveoli (last generation). There are 2
zones:
* Conducting zone
* Consists of the first 16 generations
* Incapable of gas exchange
* Respiratory zone
* Consists of the last 7 generations (17-23)
* Capable of gas exchange
Terminal bronchiole is the transition point between the conducting and respiratory zone.

Therefore it can be derived that airway resistance is inversely proportional to the radius by

With Poiseuille- Hagen formula we might feel that the smallest airways are the major site of
resistance. However, the contribution by the smallest airways is very little to the overall total
resistance. This is because, the airway branches in each generation exist in parallel rather than in
series. As the parallel branching increases, the resistance decreases. (Total cross-sectional
diameter of small airways put together is high). Thus the overall resistance of the small airways is
very small. Also, airflow velocity decreases substantially as the effective cross-sectional area
increases (i.e., the flow becomes laminar).
Other factors affecting airway resistance :
¢ Lung volume, as lung volume increases the resistance decreases and vice versa. Lung volume
increases the transairway pressure thus increasing the caliber of the airway.
« Airway mucus, edema, and contraction of bronchial smooth muscle increase the airway
resistance. Its clinical application is seen in asthma, bronchitis, and emphysema
+ The density and viscosity of inspired gas also contribute to airway resistance. A gas with more
density imparts more resistance.

questions.question: A 14-year-old boy with shortness of breath was diagnosed with chronic inflammation of conducting airways. Which of the following is not a feature of the affected structure?

options.text: Includes first 16 generations starting from trachea
Secrete variety of molecules that aid in lung defence
Membrane bound organelles namely lamellar bodies are present

questions.explanation:
Chronic inflammation of conducting airways is suggestive of asthma. Lamellar bodies are storage
bodies of surfactant present in the alveoli and not the conducting airway.
The conducting airways form the first 16 generations from the trachea to the terminal bronchial.
It is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium. It also consists of smooth muscles
which are responsible for bronchoconstriction and dilatation. It also consists of other specialized
cells such as:
+ Basal cells - stem cells
¢ Clara/Club cells - specialized epithelial cells (non-ciliated cuboidal cells) that:
+ Functions as stem cells
¢ Helps in lung defense.
The conducting airways secrete several substances that in lung defense such as:
¢ Secretory immunoglobins - IgA.
+ Collectins - surfactant protein(SP)-A and SP-D
+ Defensins
Reactive oxygen species
Reactive nitrogen species.

questions.question: Which of the following cells secrete surfactant in lungs?

suspectLines.text: + Type I cells - The primary lining cells of the alveoli (squamous epithelium); Helps in gas
Other cells — Pulmonary alveolar macrophages (PAMs/type 3 alveolar cells}, lymphocytes, plasma

questions.explanation:
Type 2 pneumocytes secrete surfactant in the lungs.
Alveolar Lining Epithelial Cells
Two types
+ Type I cells - The primary lining cells of the alveoli (squamous epithelium); Helps in gas
exchange
¢ Type II cells - Granular pneumocytes produce surfactant
Type II cells make 60% of epithelial cells in alveoli but type I cells form 95% of the total surface
area because of its flat surface.
Type II cells are stem cells which help in replenishing damaged Type 1 pneumocytes in conditions
like drug-induced pulmonary toxicity by amiodarone, bleomycin etc.
Other cells — Pulmonary alveolar macrophages (PAMs/type 3 alveolar cells}, lymphocytes, plasma
cells, neuroendocrine cells (APUD cells-Amine precursor uptake and decarboxylation), and mast
cells.

questions.question: Surfactant is composed mainly of

suspectLines.text: * Phospholipid - dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC) also known as Dipalmitoyl Lecithin.

questions.explanation:
Major surfactant is dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine i.e Lecithin. Sphingomyelin is a minor
surfactant.
The surfactant is a surface-active agent in water, which means that it greatly reduces the surface
tension of water.
Pulmonary surfactant is produced by type 2 pneumocytes.
Most important components are
* Phospholipid - dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC) also known as Dipalmitoyl Lecithin.
Lecithin is the most abundant lipid in surfactant.
+ Phosphatidylglycerol- minor component
¢ Surfactant apoproteins
* Calcium ions.
¢ 4 unique apoproteins of surfactant: surfactant protein (SP)-A, SP-B, SP-C, and SP-D.
Clinical relevance:
Tests to assess fetal lung maturity:
¢ LS ratio i.e. Lecithin/Sphingomyelin ratio: Ratio > 2 is considered normal.
¢ Shake test/Bubble test/Clement test: Formation of stable foam in the presence of surfactant.
¢ Phosphatidylglycerol levels in Amniotic fluid
¢ Autosomal dominant familial interstitial lung disease has absent surfactant protein SP-C.
¢ Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis - Autoantibody against GM-CSF which is involved in clearance of
surfactant.

questions.question: All are true of surfactant except

options.text: Deficiency of surfactant causes Infant Respiratory Distress Syndrome
Helps prevents alveolar collapse according to Bernoulli's principle
Decrease in surfactant increases the work of breathing

suspectLines.text: P - Collapsing pressure on alveolus (dynes/cm2) or Pressure required to keep alveolus open

questions.explanation:
Surfactant helps to prevent alveolar collapse according to Law of Laplace.(Not Bernoulli's)
Physiologic advantages of surfactant
¢ By reducing surface tension it increases lung compliance
¢ Reduces the lung's tendency to recoil
¢ Helps to keep the alveoli dry
¢ Helps to prevent pulmonary edema (Option A)
The surface tension generates a pressure that tends to collapse the sphere.
In accordance with Law of Laplace - P=2T/r, where
P - Collapsing pressure on alveolus (dynes/cm2) or Pressure required to keep alveolus open
(dynes/em2)
T = Surface tension (dynes/em)
r = Radius of the alveolus (cm).
Collapsing pressure is inversely related to radius i.e. large alveolus (one with a large radius) will
have a low collapsing pressure and therefore will require only minimal pressure to keep it open.
On the other hand, a small alveolus (one with a small radius) will have a high collapsing pressure
and require more pressure to keep it open.
By reducing surface tension, surfactant reduces the collapsing pressure for a given radius.
Option B: Surfactant deficiency is an important cause of infant respiratory distress syndrome
(IRDS) also known as hyaline membrane disease, the serious pulmonary disease that develops in
infants born before their surfactant system is functional.
«In IRDS, there is high surface tension in the lungs resulting in atelectasis
« Also, there is retention of fluid in the lungs.
¢ During fetal life, Cl- is secreted with fluid by the pulmonary epithelial cells. At birth, there is a
shift to Na+ reabsorption by these cells via ENaC and fluid is absorbed along with Na+. Prolonged
immaturity of ENaC contributes to pulmonary edema in IRDS.
Option D: Surfactant increases lung compliance, which reduces the work of expanding the lungs
during inspiration. Increasing the compliance of the lungs reduces the collapsing force at any
given volume so that it is easier for the lungs to expand.

questions.question: Stability of alveoli is maintained by ________.

options.text: Increased alveolar surface area by surfactant

suspectLines.text: + Pulmonary surfactant: | surface tension within alveoli

questions.explanation:
Stability of alveoli is maintained by increased alveolar surface area by surfactant.
Surfactant reduces the lung's tendency to recoil so that they do not collapse easily and so the
stability of the alveoli is maintained.
Factors that maintain alveolar stability
+ Pulmonary surfactant: | surface tension within alveoli
¢ Mechanical interdependence: prevents alveolar collapse
Interdependence
The tendency of one alveolus to collapse is opposed by the traction exerted by the surrounding
alveoli. Thus, the collapse of a single alveolus stretches and distorts the surrounding alveoli, which
in turn are connected to other alveoli. This support offered to lung units by those surrounding
them is termed Interdependence.

questions.question: A woman at risk for preterm delivery is planned for assessment of fetal lung maturity. At what gestational age will the surfactants be detectable in the amniotic fluid?

suspectLines.text: - Antenatal corticosteroids are given to increase the production of surfactants.

questions.explanation:
Surfactant appears in the amniotic fluid between 28 and 32 weeks of gestation.
By week 20-24, primitive alveoli form and surfactant production begins but it does not reach the
surface of the lungs until later.
Mature levels of pulmonary surfactant are present usually after 35 wk of gestation.
Clinical aspects :
¢ Preterm infants develop respiratory distress syndrome or hyaline membrane disease due to
surfactant deficiency.
- Antenatal corticosteroids are given to increase the production of surfactants.
¢ Lecithin/Sphingomyelin ratio is a test for fetal lung maturity. L/S ratio > 2 is suggestive of a
mature fetal lung.

questions.question: A woman on multiple medications came for an antenatal check-up. Which among the following medications that she takes decreases surfactant production?
questions.explanation:
Inadequate Insulin intake in diabetic pregnant causes inadequate glucose control. This causes
excess glucose in maternal plasma, crossing Placenta. Excess glucose in fetal plasma causes fetal
pancreas to hypersecrete fetal Insulin.
Excess insulin in fetal plasma decreases surfactant production. This is the reason for the increased
incidence of hyaline membrane disease in infants of diabetic mothers.
Factors increasing surfactant synthesis:
* Glucocorticoids
¢ Thyroxine
¢ Stretching of lungs in infancy
¢ Beta adrenergic agonist
«Calcium
¢ Regular exercise.
Factors decreasing surfactant synthesis:
¢ Smoking
¢ Long term inhalation of 100% oxygen
¢ Occlusion of main bronchus/pulmonary artery.
